newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Chinese airports to join world body.
newsitem.headline: Chinese airports to join world body.

text.p: Chinese airports, facing a dramatic surge in passenger and cargo traffic, are expected to join the world Airports Council International (ACI) shortly, according to the the Geneva-based body.

In the latest edition of its journal World Report, ACI said agreement on Chinese membership was reached during talks in July in Beijing between its Director General Oris Dunham and top officials of China's Civil Aviation Administration (CAAC).

ACI, which currently links over 430 international airports and authorities running some 1,200 airports in more than 140 countries, works to foster cooperation among its members and other partners in the world aviation industry.
Through these links, it says it also aims to help creation around the globe of an air transport system that is safe, secure, efficient and compatible with environmental norms.
Airline sources say China, whose airports are generally lagging in technological development, is keen to tap the experience and know-how it could acquire through ACI.

Four major Chinese regional airlines, which have appeared since the decentralisation of the domestic industry at the end of the 1980s, are already members of the world airline body, the International Air Traffic Association (IATA).

World Report said the CAAC officials presented Dunham with a detailed survey of their country's airport growth and the challenges they faced, especially in construction, management and pasenger and cargo facilities.
Since 1990s, the ACI journal said air traffic had increased dramatically in China and in 1995 alone eight new airports had been commissioned.

This brought the total to 129 commercial airports, of which 14 could accomodate wide-body aircraft and another 81 can handle planes up to the Boeing-737 type, the workhorse of the global airline industry which can carry between 100 and 150 passengers.

In 1995 airports all over China handled just under 100 million passengers, an increase of 27 per cent over 1994, and just under two million tonnes of cargo, up 31 per cent over the previous year, the journal said.

The top 10 airports together handled over 61 million passengers and 1.4 million tonnes of cargo in 1995 -- led by Beijing Capital with 15 million passengers, Guangzhou Baiyum with 12,5 million and Shanghai's Hongqiao with 11 million.
In cargo, Beijing came first with 371,384 tonnes, Shanghai second with 366,302 and Guangzhou third with 278,977 tones.
According to current forecasts, ACI said, passengers passing through all Chinese airports would double by the year 2000 to 200 million while cargo would surge to some four million tonnes.

But on the worldwide scale, China has a long way to go to catch up with the United States, Western European countries and Japan which currently head the ACI league for hosting the busiest airports around the globe.

In 1995, according to ACI figures, Chicago's O'Hare was the world's busiest passenger airport with just over 67 million travellers passing through. London's Heathrow was fourth with 54 million and Tokyo's Haneda sixth with 45,8 million.
In cargo, the global league was headed by Memphis International which handled 1.7 million tonnes during the year.
